subject: physics_2
question_text: What is 'Doppler effect'? Give an example.

verification.note: The 1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers, so neither check was run. Physics hand-checked: the Doppler effect is the APPARENT change in the frequency heard by an observer, caused by relative motion between source and observer — the source's own frequency never changes. Approaching train: heard frequency rises; receding: falls.

recall_prompt: Say the definition of the Doppler effect, and give the train example.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
steps.mark_note: Apparent change due to relative motion
lines: The apparent change in the frequency of
sound heard by an observer, due to
relative motion between the source and
the observer, is called the Doppler
steps.margin_note: First mark. Two phrases carry it: apparent change, and relative motion.
steps.why: The word apparent matters because the source's own frequency never changes — only what the observer HEARS changes, and only when source and observer move relative to each other.
common_mistakes: Dropping the word apparent — the emitted frequency is constant; the heard one changes.
Writing motion of the source only — relative motion of EITHER the source or the observer produces the effect.

recall.must_convey: That the Doppler effect is the apparent change in heard frequency caused by relative motion between source and observer.
accept: due to relative motion between source and observer
the heard frequency changes, not the emitted one

steps.memory_tip: Two key words: apparent (the source never changes) and relative (either one may move).

steps.label: An example
lines: approaches a person standing on the
platform, the frequency of the whistle
appears to increase. As the train moves
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Give both halves of the example — approaching AND moving away.
steps.why: Approaching motion crowds the sound waves together, so more of them reach the ear each second; receding motion spreads them out. The two halves of the example show both directions of the same effect.
common_mistakes: Saying the whistle gets louder — the Doppler effect changes the PITCH (frequency), not the loudness.

recall.must_convey: That an approaching train's whistle appears higher in frequency and a receding train's whistle lower.
accept: the pitch of the whistle changes
reject: apparent change due to relative motion

steps.memory_tip: Coming closer packs the waves — higher pitch. Going away spreads them — lower pitch.

insider_note: Frequency, not loudness — writing that the whistle gets louder is the standard way the example mark is lost.
